core: Working definition of forgetting: the failure to retrieve or retain previously learned information (APA Dictionary; typically a normal phenomenon)
The named causes of forgetting: decay, interference, retrieval failure, motivated forgetting — with the honest note that forgetting is not one single thing
The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve: memory fades fast shortly after learning, then levels off (attributed; no invented percentages)
Interference: old and new learning collide — proactive vs retroactive, each with an original example
Retrieval failure: the memory is there but unreachable (tip-of-the-tongue / blocking), with an original example
Honest framing: forgetting is often the brain working, not failing; forgetting as the mind's housekeeping
supporting: Amnesia as pathological forgetting, mentioned only to contrast with everyday forgetting
Persistence (involuntary recall of unwanted memories) mentioned only as the opposite direction
Ebbinghaus's method (nonsense syllables, relearning, 20 minutes to 30 days) as the basis of the curve

claims.claim: Forgetting is the failure to remember material that was previously learned, and it is typically a normal phenomenon rather than a disorder.
Forgetting is not one single thing: the classic accounts include decay theory and interference theory, and textbooks add retrieval failure and motivated forgetting.

Decay theory holds that learned material leaves a trace in the brain that fades and disappears over time unless the material is practiced and used; unused information tends to fade with the passage of time.

Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) studied forgetting by memorizing lists of nonsense syllables and testing himself at intervals from 20 minutes to 30 days later; his forgetting curve shows a sudden drop in retention shortly after learning followed by a more gradual decline — memory fades fast, then levels off.

Ebbinghaus's own data, reported in OpenStax Psychology 2e, showed roughly 50% of memorized material lost within about 20 minutes and about 70% within 24 hours; these figures come from his single-subject nonsense-syllable studies and are reported with attribution, not as universal laws.
Interference is the blocking of learning or of memory retrieval by the learning or remembering of other, conflicting material; stored information can be inaccessible because of it.
Proactive interference occurs when old information hinders the recall of newly learned information.
Retroactive interference occurs when information learned more recently hinders the recall of older information.
Retrieval failure (called blocking in OpenStax Psychology 2e, and central to the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon) is the inability to access stored information even though the memory is present.
Motivated forgetting is a memory lapse motivated by a desire to avoid a disagreeable recollection.
Memory failures can occur at any stage of memory (encoding, storage, retrieval), leading to forgetting — so forgetting is not evidence that the memory system is broken.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are decay and interference rival explanations of forgetting, or complementary causes?
positions: The APA Dictionary of Psychology lists decay theory and interference theory as alternative theories proposed to account for forgetting.
OpenStax Psychology 2e presents decay (storage decay) and interference as separate processes that can each explain forgetting in different situations.
The Noba Project memory module treats forgetting as failures that can occur at any stage, with interference as one mechanism among several.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents all four named causes — decay, interference, retrieval failure, and motivated forgetting — as complementary accounts that can operate alone or together, and states honestly that forgetting is not one single thing. No single cause is asserted as the exclusive explanation.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How should Ebbinghaus's classic percentages be handled?
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e reports that an average person loses 50% of memorized information after 20 minutes and 70% after 24 hours, attributed to Ebbinghaus (1885/1964).
The figures come from Ebbinghaus's own single-subject nonsense-syllable studies, not a modern population sample, and Ebbinghaus's method measured relearning savings in one participant (himself).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the figures only with attribution to Ebbinghaus as reported in OpenStax, and emphasizes the robust qualitative finding (fast drop shortly after learning, then leveling off) as the takeaway rather than presenting the exact numbers as universal laws.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no factual claims about forgetting — only generic boilerplate ('Forgetting is a foundational concept in Psychology', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') with no definitions, causes, or sources. Nothing in it was supported by research, and none of its wording was retained.
correctionsNeeded: Authored from scratch: the generated draft was generic boilerplate, so all lesson content — working definition, forgetting curve, named causes, interference types, retrieval failure, honest framing — was researched and written fresh with source support.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 8.3: Problems with Memory — OpenStax
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive snapshot (web.archive.org/web/2024id_/https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/8-3-problems-with-memory); canonical openstax.org URL registered. Supports: storage decay ('unused information tends to fade with the passage of time'); Ebbinghaus 1885 (nonsense syllables, relearning measure, 20-minute to 30-day test intervals; forgetting curve; 50%/20-min and 70%/24-h figures attributed to Ebbinghaus 1885/1964; 'memory for new information decays quickly and then eventually levels out'); interference as stored-but-inaccessible information with proactive ('old information hinders the recall of newly learned information') and retroactive ('information learned more recently hinders the recall of older information') types; blocking/tip-of-the-tongue as the inability to access stored information; persistence as involuntary recall of unwanted memories; the reassurance that everyone is prone to these memory errors. All examples in the lesson (Priya, Maya, Lena, Dario, Marcus) are original; the textbook's own examples were not reused.

sourceRecords.title: Forgetting — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Definition read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API (getdopdefinitions?q=forgetting); canonical page URL registered. Entry: 'the failure to remember material previously learned'; names decay theory and interference theory as proposed accounts; 'forgetting typically is a normal phenomenon but it may also be pathological, as, for example, in amnesia.' Anchors the lesson's working definition, the not-one-single-thing note, and the normal-not-broken framing.

sourceRecords.title: Decay theory — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Definition read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API (getdopdefinitions?q=decay-theory); canonical page URL registered. Entry: learned material 'leaves in the brain a trace or impression that autonomously recedes and disappears unless the material is practiced and used. Decay theory is a theory of forgetting.' Note: the plain slug 'decay' returns no entry; decay-theory is the correct slug. Supports the decay cause and the vocabulary definition.

sourceRecords.title: Interference — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Definition read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API (getdopdefinitions?q=interference); canonical page URL registered. Entry (memory sense): 'the blocking of learning or of memory retrieval by the learning or remembering of other conflicting material,' with sources including prior learning (proactive interference) and subsequent learning (retroactive interference). Supports the interference section and vocabulary definition.

sourceRecords.title: Proactive interference (PI) — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Definition read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API (getdopdefinitions?q=proactive-interference); canonical page URL registered. Entry: 'interference in new learning due to previous learning of similar or related material.' Supports the proactive interference definition, vocabulary entry, and Q2/Q5 keys. The dictionary's own French/Spanish example was not reused; the lesson uses an original phone-code example.

sourceRecords.title: Retroactive interference — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Definition read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API (getdopdefinitions?q=retroactive-interference); canonical page URL registered. Entry: interference 'when new learning or exposure to new information impairs the ability to remember material or carry out activities previously learned.' Supports the retroactive interference definition, vocabulary entry, and Q5 key.

sourceRecords.title: Forgetting curve — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Definition read 2026-08-22 via the dictionary's public JSON API (getdopdefinitions?q=forgetting-curve); canonical page URL registered. Entry: 'a graphic depiction of the amount of forgetting over time after learning has taken place'; Ebbinghaus, using lists of nonsense syllables, 'was the first to show that there is generally a sudden drop in retention shortly after learning, followed by a more gradual decline thereafter'; also called the Ebbinghaus curve. Supports the forgetting-curve section, vocabulary entry, and Q3 key, stated factually with attribution and no invented figures.
